newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - Grain prices fall on USDA report, cotton up.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Grain prices fall on USDA report, cotton up.

text.p: Grain prices fell sharply on Wednesday after the U.S. Agriculture Department's monthly Supply/Demand Report but analysts said big questions about end-season crop conditions should keep prices underpinned.
"For the big picture the report is supportive for oilseeds but bearish for wheat and feedgrains," said Dan Cekander, head of grain research for trade house FIMAT Futures USA Inc.
Wheat prices led the declines after USDA predicted an increase in 1996 U.S. wheat production, a hike in 1996-97 wheat ending stocks and higher Australian wheat production.

CBOT September wheat was down 8-1/4 cents a bushel in early trading at $4.44-1/2, with December corn down 4-1/4 cents at $3.30. November soybeans fell three cents to $8.04, before rebounding somewhat.

USDA raised its 1996 corn crop estimate to 8.804 billion bushels and lowered its soybean crop estimate to 2.270 billion bushels, from 8.695 billion bushels and 2.300 billion bushels, respectively, estimated a month ago.
Last year, the U.S. produced 7.374 billion bushels of corn and 2.152 billion bushels of soybeans.
It raised wheat production to 2.296 billion bushels from 2.249 billion last month.

Analysts said the market responded most strongly to USDA's revised higher estimates for end-season stocks next year. USDA predicted corn stocks on Sept 1, 1997, would be 668 million bushels, up from 523 million last month and 409 million on September 1, 1996.
Wheat stocks next July were seen at 506 million bushels, up from 409 million last month and 375 million a year earlier.
But soybean stocks as of Sept 1, 1997, were seen falling further to 160 million bushels from 175 million estimated last month and 170 million a year earlier -- a bullish factor.
Cotton futures soared after USDA cut production and stocks estimates.

The USDA put 1996 cotton production at 17.9 million bales, down from 18.58 million seen last month and unchanged from last year's 17.9 million. The end-season cotton stocks forecast was lowered to 3.60 million bales from 4.00 million seen last month.
December cotton at the New York Cotton Exchange opened locked up the daily 3.00-cent a lb limit at 76.07 cents.
"It's very much of a surprise, the production data," said Prudential Securities cotton specialist Ernest Simon. "It is much lower than expected."
And CBOT grain analysts were quick to caution against any great selloff, since poor weather continues to hamper crops.

Indeed, analysts said U.S. Midwest weather patterns over the next 30 days or so will be critical to the fate of corn and soybean yields, with the bulk of plants from Ohio to Nebraska now maturing amid cooler-than-desired temperatures.

"It's a supportive situation. We've been dry during (soybean) pod filing and the October report will probably show a decline in production," Prudential Securities vice president Rod Engle told reporters after the release of USDA's estimates.
"The bean number to me is constructive," Cekander said. "The bean carryout was lowered, so for the longer term, we should go higher," he said.
Agriculture officials in Illinois, usually the number one or two soybean state, underscored the cautious outlook toward any optimism after the USDA data.

"Dry weather during much of August prevented additional pods from setting as well as limiting the filling of pods. The crop is two to three weeks behind normal," the Illinois Department of Agriculture said in a release.
It said rain in mid-August aided the Illinois corn crop but "the moderate temperatures were also a disadvantage to the crop in that development was somewhat slower than normal."
Meterologists on Wednesday morning also brought jitters, predicting a cold front for the eastern Corn Belt this week.
"There is some chilly weather around," said Mike Palmerino, meteorologist with Weather Services Corp. "It appears as though it is going to be moving across the Midwest in the next couple of days."
Highs were seen in the mid- to upper-50s Fahrenheit to low 60s, said Basilio Lopez, meteorologist with Smith Barney.
"The cooler air will slow down late pod development throughout the Midwest," Lopez said. "Little threat of frost is foreseen through the coming weekend and into next week."
